cloud-models-and-shared-responsibility.title: Welcome to Cloud models and the shared-responsibility boundary, part of Cloud Security.
cloud-models-and-shared-responsibility.idea: Most serious cloud incidents are not caused by a failure of the provider's data centres. They are caused by a customer setting that was left open, a credential that was copied into the wrong place, or a service that was assumed to be private. The provider's security is extensive, but it is bounded, and the customer's part is the part that is most often misunderstood. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and the boundary. The rest of the course applies them to identities, networks, data, posture and response.
cloud-models-and-shared-responsibility.example: A team uses a managed database service. The provider encrypts the storage, patches the engine and replicates the data across availability zones. A developer wants to connect from a laptop, so the team sets the database's network rule to allow connections from anywhere, and creates one shared username and password. Trace the responsibilities: 1. Provider: the storage is encrypted at rest, and the engine is patched. Nothing the provider did was wrong. 2. Customer, network: the rule allowing any source address is the customer's configuration. The database is now reachable from the internet, which is the provider's default for a service that a customer chose to expose. 3. Customer, identity: a shared account with a password that is also in a repository means that no one can be identified in the logs and anyone with the repository can connect. 4. Customer, data: whether the data is classified as personal data determines what notification duties apply if it is exposed. The fix is entirely in the customer's column: a private network address, an identity per person or per workload, the password moved into a secrets store, and logs turned on and reviewed. The provider could not have prevented any of these decisions.
cloud-models-and-shared-responsibility.challenge: For a small fictional application (a web front end, an API and a managed database), write a shared-responsibility table for its deployment, a list of the five decisions the customer must make, and the account structure that contains the blast radius. Then identify the one decision in your design that would most increase risk if it were made carelessly, and explain the control that protects against it.

identity-and-access-management.title: Welcome to Identity and access management, part of Cloud Security.
identity-and-access-management.idea: Cloud authorisation is built from four parts. A principal is the identity making a request: a human user, a role assumed temporarily, or a service. An action is the operation requested, such as s3:GetObject (read an object) or iam:CreateAccessKey. A resource is what the action applies to, identified by an Amazon Resource Name (ARN). A condition narrows when the rule applies, such as only when multi-factor authentication is present or only from a particular network. A policy is a document that grants or denies combinations of these. Azure expresses the same idea with role assignments (a role, a principal and a scope) and Microsoft Entra ID for identities; Google Cloud uses IAM bindings on resources. The vocabulary differs, but the principle of granting specific actions on specific resources is the same. The principle of least privilege says that a principal should have exactly the actions it needs on exactly the resources it uses, and nothing more. It is easy to state and hard to achieve, which is why the rest of this lesson is about finding the gap between what is granted and what is used.
identity-and-access-management.example: The policy below grants read access to one prefix of one bucket, and only to principals who have signed in with multi-factor authentication within the last hour. Read it as a checklist. 1. Effect: Allow grants what follows; an explicit Deny in any applicable policy always overrides an allow. 2. Action lists the single operation needed, not s3:. 3. Resource names one bucket and one prefix, using the ARN form. A wildcard on the bucket would grant access to every bucket in the account. 4. Condition requires a recent MFA sign-in, so a stolen long-lived password alone is not enough. An over-permissive version of the same grant would use "Action": "s3:" and "Resource": "*". It would work in testing and would give an attacker with the same credentials the ability to read, change and delete every bucket in the account.
identity-and-access-management.challenge: In a lab account, design an identity model for three roles: a developer who deploys to a non-production environment, a build pipeline that deploys to production, and an auditor who reads logs but changes nothing. Write the policies, the trust relationships and the MFA requirements. Then use the simulator to prove that each role can do its job and cannot do the others' jobs, and attach the results to your design.

network-and-workload-protection.title: Welcome to Network and workload protection, part of Cloud Security.
network-and-workload-protection.idea: The most common cloud exposure is not sophisticated. It is a database or an administrative port that was opened to every address during a fault investigation and never closed. Network design is the discipline of making that kind of mistake hard to make and easy to find. The principle is layered: a workload should have no route to the internet unless it needs one, and each route should carry only the traffic it needs. The lesson applies to virtual machines, managed services and containers alike, because they all sit inside a virtual network with rules that someone wrote.
network-and-workload-protection.example: A web application runs on a virtual machine. During an outage, an engineer adds a security group rule allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 (any address) so that they can log in from home. The outage is fixed; the rule remains. Trace what an attacker sees: 1. A scanner on the internet probes the public address and finds port 22 open. The response is a banner identifying the SSH server version. 2. The attacker tries common usernames and passwords. If the instance allows password authentication, the attempts are only limited by the attacker's patience. 3. Automated scanning of the cloud provider's address ranges means that this exposure is found within hours of creation, not weeks. The defender's version of the same trace reads the audit records. A rule creation event for the security group, made by an identity that normally does not change firewall rules, is the signal. The corrective controls are: remove the rule, use session-manager access instead, require key-only authentication, and add a policy that alerts on any rule that opens a sensitive port to the whole internet.
network-and-workload-protection.challenge: Build a three-tier network in a lab account with a public load balancer, a private application tier and a private database. Use session-manager access only. Then produce an audit script that fails if any security group allows a sensitive port from the internet, and demonstrate that it fails on a deliberately bad change and passes on the corrected design.

data-protection-and-secrets.title: Welcome to Data protection and secrets, part of Cloud Security.
data-protection-and-secrets.idea: Data protection has three questions: where is the data, who can read it, and what happens if a copy is taken. Encryption answers the second question only if the keys are controlled. Secrets management answers it for credentials. Backups answer the third, but only if an attacker who controls the production system cannot also destroy the backups. Privacy law adds a fourth question: is the data necessary at all?
data-protection-and-secrets.example: Customer-managed encryption, set and then verified: The worked example shows the idea in code.
data-protection-and-secrets.challenge: Design the data protection for a fictional clinic's patient-booking application. Specify the storage encryption and key policy, the secrets flow from store to application, the backup and restore design with immutability, the data inventory and retention periods, and the cross-border transfer position under the Data Protection Act. Demonstrate the technical controls in a lab with synthetic records and attach the command evidence.

posture-and-infrastructure-as-code.title: Welcome to Cloud security posture and infrastructure as code, part of Cloud Security.
posture-and-infrastructure-as-code.idea: Security reviews of cloud environments usually find the same handful of problems: public storage, over-permissive roles, unencrypted disks, logging turned off, and resources in regions nobody reviews. These are not exotic. They are the predictable result of creating infrastructure by hand, quickly, under pressure, and never checking it again. The answer is to make the checks automatic and to run them at the point where a change is proposed.
posture-and-infrastructure-as-code.example: A developer writes the following Terraform for a reports bucket and a firewall rule. Before it runs, the pipeline executes a static analysis tool. Read the file, then the findings that a tool such as Checkov would raise, then the corrected version.
posture-and-infrastructure-as-code.challenge: Create a Terraform project for a small web application with a public load balancer, a private database and a reports bucket. Enforce the benchmark with Checkov in a CI workflow, write one custom policy for your organisation's tagging standard, and show a pull request that fails the check and one that passes. Document every exception with its owner and review date.

cloud-detection-and-response.title: Welcome to Cloud detection and incident response, part of Cloud Security.
cloud-detection-and-response.idea: Traditional incident response assumes that you can disconnect a machine and examine its disk. In a cloud account the attacker often never touches a machine. They use a valid credential to call the platform's API, create a new user, an access key or a virtual machine, and leave. The evidence is in the audit trail, and the response is to revoke access to the identity and check everything it touched. This is faster than a disk investigation and more demanding in its logging requirements.
cloud-detection-and-response.example: A secret scanner alerts that a long-lived access key for the user reports-sync appeared in a public repository commit made four hours ago. The response runs in a fixed order, because each step protects the evidence needed for the next. 1. Contain the identity first. Deactivate the access key (aws iam update-access-key --status Inactive). Do not delete it yet, because deletion removes the link between the key and its history in some views. Attach a deny policy to the user if it has other keys or a console password. 2. Establish the timeline. Find the key's identifier, then search the audit trail for every action it took. Start from the first event in the commit's window, not from the alert time. 3. Look for persistence. Search for identity and policy changes made by the same principal: new users, new access keys, new roles, changes to trust policies, and changes to security groups or logging configuration. 4. Check for impact. Review data access events for the storage services the user could reach, and review compute and network creation events for mining or exfiltration. 5. Eradicate. Delete any persistence found, delete the compromised key, and remove the secret from the repository history. Rotate any other credential the attacker could have read. 6. Restore and recover. Replace the key with a role assumed through the build system's identity, scoped to the deployment actions only. 7. Review. Record the timeline, the detection gap (why the key was in the repository in the first place), and the actions with owners. In a real case the step that is most often skipped is step 3. A deleted key with a surviving backdoor user is a re-entry waiting to happen.
cloud-detection-and-response.challenge: Write a complete incident-response playbook for a leaked cloud access key, with the commands for containment, the audit queries for scoping and persistence, the eradication checklist and the review template. Run it against a lab key, time each step, and attach the timeline and the evidence. Identify the one step you would most want to automate, and explain why.
